Doing the right thing even when no one is watching, no police are nearby, and no one is there to scold you is the path to a better life. Don't let your heart become rigid like an overinflated tire. By choosing to give way and offer kindness, you ensure that your heart remains soft, resilient, and truly noble.

Imagine if you could take a trip to a beautiful, golden palace without spending a single penny. Usually, exciting trips cost a lot of money, but there is a secret way to reach a wonderful place called "heaven" for free. That secret is called humility. Humility means being respectful to others and keeping your heart gentle instead of proud.

Some people think they are too important to show respect to anyone. This kind of pride makes a person’s heart hard and stiff, like a car tire that has been pumped with too much air. This stubborn attitude doesn't help anyone; in fact, it can lead to a very unhappy future.

Many years ago, in a city called Rajgir, there lived an elderly woman named Candali. She was incredibly poor and had to beg for food every day, leaning on a shaky wooden stick. One morning, the Buddha looked out at the world with his great wisdom and saw that Candali’s life was almost over. He saw that if she didn't do something good soon, she would have a very difficult journey after she passed away. Because the Buddha was so kind, he decided to walk down the road where she was begging to help her.

When they met, the Buddha’s disciple, Moggallana, realized what the Buddha was planning. He encouraged the old woman, saying, "Your time in this world is short. Quickly, show your respect to the Great Buddha!"

Even though Candali was poor, she could have been stubborn. She could have refused to bow. But she was wise. She dropped her walking stick, knelt on the ground, and bowed three times at the Buddha’s feet. Her heart was filled with peace and joy.

Later that same day, a tragic accident happened, and Candali passed away. Because her very last thoughts were filled with respect and kindness toward the Buddha, she didn't go to a sad place. Instead, she was reborn as a beautiful angel in heaven! She even came back that night as a radiant being to thank Moggallana for his advice.

What can we learn from Candali’s story for our own lives?

1. Showing respect makes you a noble person. Being polite to your parents, listening to your teachers, or giving up your seat for an elder doesn't cost any money, but it changes who you are inside. It makes your heart soft and kind. People who are humble are often more loved and respected by everyone they meet.

2. Focus on your "inner software." Today, many people have fancy "hardware" like the newest phones or cool clothes. But if someone talks loudly on their phone in a quiet place or plays loud music without thinking of others, their inner software needs an upgrade! Good manners and being thoughtful are what truly make a person stand out.

3. Respect public spaces. A public park or a bus belongs to everyone, so we should treat these places with care. This means not throwing trash on the ground and being quiet so we don't disturb others. Real character is doing the right thing even when no one is watching, like keeping a piece of trash in your pocket until you find a bin.

Don't be like a stiff, over-inflated tire. Instead, be like Candali. Keep your heart gentle, respect those around you, and always try to be a kind neighbor to the world.

Imagine holding a soccer ball or a bicycle tire. When they are empty, the rubber is soft and flexible. But what happens when you pump them full of air? They become hard and stiff. Our minds work the same way. When we fill our hearts with pride—thinking "I am the best" or "I am smarter than everyone else"—our minds become rigid like that over-inflated tire. This pride makes us lose our kindness and respect for others, making us feel as though we are better than everyone else.

Pride is a dangerous thing because it hurts us before it hurts anyone else. Think of it this way: if you pick up a handful of mud to throw at someone, your own hands get dirty first. Even if you miss your target, you are already covered in filth. In the same way, the moment you look down on someone, your heart becomes unkind and unpleasant.

To understand how dangerous pride can be, let’s look at two stories from the past:

1. Prince Dutthakumara: He was a very proud and angry young man. One day, while he was traveling to his gardens, he met a wise and peaceful monk called a Paccekabuddha. All the people on the street stopped to bow and show respect to the monk, but they didn't pay much attention to the prince. This made the prince feel very insulted. In a fit of pride and rage, he grabbed the monk’s food bowl, smashed it on the ground, and stepped on the food. Because he was so disrespectful to such a holy person, he faced terrible consequences for his actions and lost everything.

2. Sunita: In one of his past lives, he was very arrogant and hung out with the wrong crowd. When he saw a monk walking by, he didn't show respect. Instead, he yelled, "Why don't you go clean toilets or scoop up trash instead of asking for food?" Because he looked down on others so much, he spent many future lives working as a waste collector. People treated him poorly, just as he had done to others. It was only after he met the Buddha and learned to be humble that he finally found peace and became a respected monk himself.

Pride doesn't just happen in ancient stories; we see it in our daily lives as a lack of "Civic Sense." This is a form of pride because people put their own wants above the comfort of everyone else. Examples include:

- Talking loudly on a phone or playing music without headphones on a bus.

- Smoking in public places.

- Tossing trash on the street.

True respect and civic sense mean doing the right thing even when no one is watching. It means waiting for the red light even if there are no police nearby, or keeping your trash in your bag until you find a bin. We should always have two things in our hearts:

- "Hiri": The shame of doing wrong.

- "Ottappa": The fear of the results of doing wrong.

Instead of letting our hearts become hard and stiff like an over-inflated tire, let’s try to keep them soft and kind. By being humble and thinking of others, we make the world a better place for everyone.

Have you ever felt like you were smarter, cooler, or more important than someone else? That feeling is called pride. But here is a secret: whenever we look down on others, our own hearts become "dirty" before we even say a word. Think of it like this: if you pick up a handful of mud to throw at someone, your own hands get muddy first, whether you hit the target or not. Pride is just like that mud.

Long ago, in a time before our current Buddha, a young man who would later become Sunita lived a life full of pride. He hung out with the wrong people and had a very stubborn, mean attitude. One day, a holy person called a Silent Buddha came to his village to collect food. Instead of being respectful, the young man became angry. He shouted cruel words at the holy man:

- "Why are you begging for food? Go get a real job!"

- "If you can't farm or trade, go clean out people’s toilets and carry away their waste instead!"

Because he insulted a good person so cruelly, Sunita’s life became very difficult. After facing a long time of suffering, he spent many, many lifetimes being born into the poorest families. In those days, his job was always the one he had joked about: a waste scavenger. He was the person who had to clean the filth from the city. He wore old clothes, never had enough to eat, and everyone looked down on him. Because he had been so proud in the past, he now had to live a life where he had to bow and be humble to everyone he met just to survive.

In his very last life, Sunita was born in the city of Rajagaha. He was still a poor waste collector. One morning, the Buddha saw with his special wisdom that Sunita was ready to change his life. The Buddha walked into the narrow, dirty alley where Sunita was working. When Sunita saw the Buddha and his monks, he was terrified! He thought he was too "unclean" to be near them. He tried to hide against a wall, holding his waste buckets out of the way.

But the Buddha walked right up to him and spoke with a voice as sweet as honey. "Sunita," the Buddha asked, "this work is so hard and sad. Would you like to leave it behind and become a monk?" Sunita was so happy he could hardly believe it. He joined the Buddha, practiced meditation with great focus, and eventually became an Arhat—a fully enlightened person. Even the most powerful kings came to bow to him because his heart was finally pure.

What can we learn from Sunita’s story today? It teaches us about something called "Civic Sense." Sometimes, we are very polite to teachers or famous people, but we might be rude to a janitor or a person cleaning the street. If we walk across a freshly mopped floor with muddy shoes without caring, are we really being respectful?

- True character is how you treat people when no one is watching.

- Having a fancy phone or expensive clothes is like having nice "hardware," but having a kind and helpful heart is like having the best "software" inside you.

- Don't let your heart get puffed up with air like a tire.

- Instead, remember to respect everyone's hard work, no matter who they are or what they do.

Have you ever wondered why Buddhists celebrate Metta Day on the full moon day of Wagaung? Long ago, the Buddha taught a very special lesson called the Metta Sutta on this day. This is the story of how that teaching began.

During the time of the Buddha, 500 monks learned meditation and traveled to a large, quiet forest to practice. In that forest, there were many spirits called devas who lived in the trees. Because the monks were so virtuous, the devas felt they had to move out of their tree homes and stay on the ground to show respect. At first, the devas didn't mind, but as the days passed, they became uncomfortable and wanted their homes back.

To drive the monks away, the devas began to haunt them. At night, they made terrifying noises and showed the monks frightening, ghostly images. The monks were so scared that they could no longer focus on their meditation. After a month of struggling, they returned to the Buddha at Jetavana Monastery and told him about the scary things they had seen.

The Buddha listened kindly and said, "My students, you went to the forest without your shield of protection. That shield is Metta, which means loving-kindness. You must go back to that same forest, but this time, take this weapon of love with you." He then taught them the Metta Sutta, a chant about sending love to all living things.

The monks returned to the forest and began practicing what the Buddha had taught. They sent thoughts of love and peace to every creature and spirit in the woods. A wonderful transformation happened! The spirits felt the monks' kindness and stopped being scary. Instead of haunting the monks, the devas became their friends and even helped them with their daily chores. Because they were finally at peace, all 500 monks were able to reach enlightenment.

There are three important things to remember from this story:

1. Metta Day falls on the full moon of Wagaung to honor the day the Buddha shared this teaching.

2. Metta is the strongest protection we have. When we face scary situations, responding with kindness is often the best way to stay safe.

3. Love has the power to change others. When you treat people with a heart full of love, even those who seem like enemies can become your friends.

You can practice this in your own life too. Every morning or before you go to sleep, try thinking:

- "May all beings be free from danger."

- "May they be happy and peaceful."

When you share your love with the world this way, you will find that you sleep better, have fewer bad dreams, and feel more loved by the people around you.

Metta is the ultimate shield against fear and hostility.

Every day when you travel on a bus, a train, or walk down a busy street, there are "secret tests" for your heart. These tests happen whenever you see an elderly person, a pregnant mother, or someone who deserves respect, like a monk or a teacher. How you react in these moments shows what kind of person you are becoming.

Some people grab a seat on the bus and then pretend to be busy on their phones so they don't have to give it up to someone else. Some people refuse to move aside on the sidewalk and might even bump into others on purpose. Why do people act this way? It is because of something called "Pride." In your heart, pride feels like a car tire that has been pumped way too full of air. It makes your mind stiff and hard, making you think, "Why should I move? I was here first!"

The Buddha once shared an important lesson called the Sula Kamma Vibhanga Sutta. He explained that if we constantly act bossy, refuse to give up our seats, or show no respect to those who deserve it, our hearts become harsh and low. He taught that:

- This negative behavior can lead to a very unhappy future.

- Even if a proud person is born as a human again, they might find themselves in a life where they have no respect and are looked down upon by others.

Think about this: giving up your seat or stepping aside to let someone pass doesn't cost you a single cent. It is a "pot of gold" that you can get for free! While it costs nothing, it makes the other person feel peaceful and happy. At the same time, you are filling your own heart with "Kutho" (merit) and building a beautiful culture. The Buddha said that people who are respectful and kind will find happiness in the future and will be born into respected, noble families where everyone honors them.

We should also think about why we are being polite. Are we only respectful to people with power, like a police officer or a boss, because we are afraid of them? Real "Civic Sense" means respecting everyone, even people you don't know.

- If you see someone cleaning the floor and you walk over it with muddy shoes without caring about their hard work, you aren't being truly respectful.

- True kindness is about valuing every human being’s effort, not just being afraid of authority.

In today’s world, you might have a fancy phone or cool gadgets. Think of these as your "Hardware." But if you use that phone to play loud music on a bus or shout while others are trying to rest, your "Software"—your inner mindset—needs an update. Having high-quality "Software" means:

- Caring about the peace and quiet of the people around you.

- Not littering.

- Understanding that public spaces belong to everyone, so we must share them with kindness.

Real character is doing the right thing even when no one is watching and no one is there to catch you. It comes from having a healthy sense of:

1. "Hiri": Feeling embarrassed to do something bad.

2. "Ottappa": Knowing that bad actions have bad consequences.

So, the next time you are out, don’t let your heart stay stiff like an over-inflated tire. Be the person who moves aside and offers a seat. By doing this, you keep your heart soft, kind, and beautiful.

Do you want to be a person that others truly respect? Many people believe that being "high class" means having power, being rich, or acting like they are better than everyone else. They let their pride grow big, like a tire overfilled with air. But the Buddha taught something very different. He said that true greatness comes from being humble and showing respect to others. When we are too proud, our hearts become stiff and cold, which actually makes us less honorable people.

Long ago, in the kingdom of Kapilavatthu, there were six famous Sakyian princes. These princes, including Bhaddiya and Ananda, were very proud of their royal family and their high status. They had a servant named Upali who worked as their barber. One day, the six princes decided to leave their wealthy lives behind to become monks and follow the Buddha. As they reached the forest, they took off their expensive jewelry and gave it all to Upali. They told him to take the treasures home and live a comfortable life.

Upali started to walk back with the jewelry, but he stopped to think. He realized that if these powerful princes could give up their kingdoms to find peace, why should he cling to a bag of gold? He also worried that if people saw a servant with royal jewels, they might think he had hurt the princes to steal them. Upali decided to hang the jewelry on a tree branch and ran back to join the princes. He wanted to become a monk, too.

When they arrived to see the Buddha, the princes made a very special and surprising request. They knew that their biggest problem was their own pride. They said:

* "Buddha, we Sakyians are very stubborn and proud."

* "Upali has been our servant for a long time."

* "Please ordain Upali as a monk first, before you ordain us."

Why did they ask for this? In the monkhood, members show respect to whoever joined before them. By making Upali a monk first, the princes—who used to be his masters—would have to bow down and show him respect. This was their way of crushing their own ego and learning true humility. The Buddha was pleased with their honesty and did exactly what they asked. The princes successfully conquered their pride by bowing to their former servant, and one of them, Bhaddiya, eventually became recognized as one of the most excellent monks.

We can learn a lot from this for our own lives today. Pride doesn't just belong to ancient princes; it lives in us, too. Sometimes we feel "better" than others because:

1. We have a newer phone.

2. We live in a big house.

3. We have parents with high-ranking jobs.

Using these things to look down on others is like having fancy "hardware" but broken "software" inside your heart.

True "Civic Sense" means respecting the rights of everyone, especially people we don’t know. For example, some people talk loudly on their phones or play videos on a speaker in a public bus. They think, "It’s my phone and my money, so I can do what I want." This is a type of pride. It means they only care about themselves and ignore the peace and quiet that the other passengers deserve.

Real character is about how you act when no one is watching. It means:

* Stopping at a red light even if there is no police officer.

* Keeping your trash in your pocket until you find a bin instead of dropping it on the street.

This comes from two important feelings:

Hiri*: The shame of doing something wrong.

Ottappa*: The fear of the consequences of doing wrong.

Today, we are going to learn a very different story about what happens when someone lets pride and anger take over. This is the historical story of King Suppabuddha, a ruler who learned a terrifying lesson about blocking someone else’s path.

King Suppabuddha was the ruler of a kingdom called Devadaha. He was actually the Buddha’s uncle, but he held two very deep grudges in his heart:

- First, he was angry that the Buddha had left his daughter, Princess Yasodhara, to become a monk.

- Second, he was upset that his son, Devadatta, had also become a monk and was now a rival to the Buddha.

Because of these feelings, the King’s heart became hard and full of stubborn pride.

One day, the King decided to cause trouble. He knew the Buddha and his monks would be walking down a specific road to collect their morning meals. To show off his power, the King sat right in the middle of the road, drinking alcohol and refusing to move. When people asked him to clear the way for the Buddha, he shouted, "I will not move! He is younger than me, so why should I give him the path?" Because the King refused to be fair, the Buddha kindly turned back and went another way.

After this happened, the Buddha told his assistant, Ananda, that the King’s actions would have a serious consequence. He predicted that in seven days, the earth would open up and swallow the King at the bottom of his palace stairs.

When the King heard this, he thought he could outsmart the Buddha and prove him wrong. He took the following precautions:

1. He moved to the very top floor of his seven-story palace.

2. He had all the stairs removed.

3. He locked every door and hired strong wrestlers to guard them.

4. He told the guards, "If you see me trying to go downstairs, stop me and pull me back!"

The Buddha explained that it didn't matter if the King hid in a palace, flew into the sky, or hid in a cave—the truth of the Buddha’s words never changes. On the seventh day, the King’s favorite royal horse began to act wild and terrified in the courtyard below. The horse was kicking the walls and making a loud, scary noise. This horse would only calm down for the King.

In a moment of panic and forgetfulness, the King jumped up to go down to his horse. Suddenly, the removed stairs reappeared in their places, and the locked doors swung wide open. The guards, instead of stopping the King, felt confused and actually pushed him toward the exit. As soon as the King reached the bottom of the stairs and his feet touched the ground, the earth cracked open. King Suppabuddha was swallowed by the ground and fell straight into a place of great suffering called Avici Hell.

This story teaches us several important lessons for our own lives:

- Having a "me first" attitude is dangerous. King Suppabuddha blocked a road just because he was angry. Today, we see people doing similar things, like parking cars where they block traffic or playing music so loud that it disturbs the whole neighborhood. Being selfish and ignoring the rights of others is a sign of a person who lacks "civic sense."

- Pride and anger make our hearts hard. When we think we are better than everyone else, we stop caring about being kind.

- We should practice having a sense of shame and fear regarding doing wrong. This means doing the right thing even when no one is watching or when there are no police around to stop us. Real character means following the rules and being helpful because you care about your community.

Let’s remember to keep our hearts soft and kind. Instead of blocking others or letting pride get in the way, we should always try to be helpful and respectful to everyone we meet.

Sometimes we think we are better than others. This is called being proud. But being proud can hurt us. Think of it like this: if you pick up mud to throw at someone, your hands get dirty first! When we are mean to others, our hearts get dirty first.

Long ago, there was a boy named Sunita. He was a very mean boy. One day, he saw a holy monk. Instead of being kind, Sunita laughed at him. He told the monk, "Go clean toilets!" This was a very mean thing to say.

Because Sunita was so mean, his life became very hard:

Lesson
- He had to work as a waste cleaner for a long time.

- He was very poor and had to wear old clothes.

- People were not nice to him, and he had to bow to everyone he met.

Lesson
- He felt very sad and low.

One morning, the Great Buddha saw Sunita. The Buddha was very kind. He went to the place where Sunita was working. Sunita was scared because he thought he was not important. He tried to hide, but the Buddha walked right up to him.

The Buddha spoke in a sweet voice. He asked, "Sunita, would you like to be a monk?" Sunita was so happy! He joined the Buddha and worked hard to be good. Soon, he became a very wise and holy man.

Lesson
We can learn a big lesson from Sunita:

1. We should never look down on people.

2. It does not matter if someone is rich or poor.

Lesson
3. It does not matter what job they do.

4. We should be kind to the people who clean the streets just like we are kind to our teachers.

Having a kind heart is like having a beautiful light inside you. Do not be like a hard tire full of air. Instead, be soft and gentle. Let’s be kind to everyone we meet today!
